summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\), one of \((2,17),(3,17),(5,23),(7,19),(11,13)\) consists of primes \(q,r\) neither dividing \(d\), with \(qr\le150\) and different final digits. Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(qr\), some index \(0\le i<qr\) makes \(a+id\) divisible by both \(q\) and \(r\), so one of the first 150 terms has prime divisors with different final digits.

full_proof.text:
We prove that the asserted arithmetic progression cannot exist.

Call an integer greater than 1 lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same residue modulo 10. We will use the following five pairs of primes:
\[
(2,17),\qquad (3,17),\qquad (5,23),\qquad (7,19),\qquad (11,13).
\]
The relevant data are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
q&r&qr&(q\bmod 10,r\bmod 10)\\ \hline
2&17&34&(2,7)\\
3&17&51&(3,7)\\
5&23&115&(5,3)\\
7&19&133&(7,9)\\
11&13&143&(1,3).
\end{array}
\]
Thus, in every row, both entries are prime, their final decimal digits differ, and their product is at most 150. (Primality here is immediate by trial division by primes no larger than the relevant square roots.)

We first establish the key covering fact about possible common differences.

**Lemma.** For every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\), at least one of the five displayed pairs \((q,r)\) has the property that neither \(q\) nor \(r\) divides \(d\).

**Proof.** Suppose instead that every pair has at least one member dividing \(d\). We split according to whether 17 divides \(d\).

If \(17\nmid d\), then the pair \((2,17)\) forces \(2\mid d\), and the pair \((3,17)\) forces \(3\mid d\). The remaining three pairs force the existence of primes
\[
s\in\{5,23\},\qquad t\in\{7,19\},\qquad u\in\{11,13\}
\]
with \(s\mid d\), \(t\mid d\), and \(u\mid d\). The five primes \(2,3,s,t,u\) are distinct. Consequently they are pairwise coprime, so their product divides \(d\). Since \(s\ge5\), \(t\ge7\), and \(u\ge11\), this gives
\[
d\ge 2\cdot3\cdot s\cdot t\cdot u
   \ge 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11
   =2310,
\]
contrary to \(d\le2025\).

If \(17\mid d\), the last three pairs again provide primes
\[
s\in\{5,23\},\qquad t\in\{7,19\},\qquad u\in\{11,13\}
\]
which divide \(d\). These primes and 17 are all distinct, hence their product divides \(d\). It follows that
\[
d\ge17stu\ge17\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=6545,
\]
again contradicting \(d\le2025\). This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Now suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) satisfying
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025,
\]
and such that all 150 integers
\[
a,
 a+d,
 a+2d,
 \ldots,
 a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

Apply the lemma to \(d\), and choose one of the five pairs \((q,r)\) such that
\[
q\nmid d\quad\hbox{and}\quad r\nmid d.
\]
Because \(q\) and \(r\) are distinct primes, neither dividing \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,q)=\gcd(d,r)=1,
\]
and therefore
\[
\gcd(d,qr)=1.
\]
Set \(N=qr\). Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(N\), the congruence
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod N
\]
has a solution modulo \(N\): explicitly, if \(d^{-1}\) denotes the inverse of \(d\) modulo \(N\), take
\[
i\equiv-a d^{-1}\pmod N.
\]
Choose the unique representative with
\[
0\le i<N.
\]
For this representative,
\[
N=qr\mid a+id.
\]
The table shows that \(N=qr\le150\), so
\[
0\le i<N\le150,
\]
which means \(0\le i<150\). Thus \(a+id\) is one of the asserted 150 terms of the progression.

On the other hand, \(qr\mid a+id\) implies separately that
\[
q\mid a+id\qquad\text{and}\qquad r\mid a+id.
\]
Both \(q\) and \(r\) are therefore prime divisors of this term. Their final decimal digits differ, as recorded in the last column of the table. Hence the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all have the same final decimal digit. In other words, \(a+id\) is not lopsided. Notice also that
\[
a+id\ge a\ge2,
\]
so there is no issue involving 0 or 1: this term lies in exactly the range to which the definition of lopsided applies.

We have found among the first 150 terms a term that is not lopsided, contradicting the assumption that all of them occur in A381159. Therefore there are no integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which every \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), belongs to A381159. This disproves the conjecture.
